subject: chemistry
title: Chromatography and Magnetism
welcome_lead: Split rainbow inks with paper, or pluck iron out of a pile with a magnet.
meta_desc: Use chromatography and magnetism to separate mixtures in this KS3 chemistry adventure.
final_note: You can now choose the right separation method for any mixture.

walkthroughs.body_html:
Chromatography separates the different coloured dyes in inks. Dot the ink on paper, dip the bottom in solvent (often water), and watch the colours spread up the paper at different speeds.

Each dye forms its own spot. A pure dye gives just one spot.

A simple way to remove iron from a mixture is to use a magnet. Iron, cobalt and nickel are magnetic; most other materials are not.

Iron filings out of sand.

Ask: are the parts solid or liquid? Can they dissolve? Are any magnetic?

Filtration for insoluble solids, evaporation for soluble solids, distillation for liquids, chromatography for dyes, and magnets for iron.

mcqs.q: In an exothermic reaction, what happens energetically with the bonds?
options: The reactants get colder because they lose mass as energy.
The number of peaks equals the total number of protons in the molecule.
Bond breaking releases energy and bond making absorbs energy.
Energy released forming new bonds exceeds energy absorbed breaking existing bonds.

mcqs.q: Can a single standard electrode potential be measured in isolation?
options: The number of peaks equals the total number of protons in the molecule.
Standard electrode potentials are measured by submerging the electrode in pure water.
Each electrode has an absolute potential that can be measured directly with a voltmeter.
No — electrode potentials are RELATIVE values measured against a reference (the standard hydrogen electrode, defined as 0 V).

mcqs.q: In 1H NMR, what does the n+1 rule predict?
options: The number of peaks equals the total number of protons in the molecule.
Splitting tells you how many protons are in the same chemical environment as the one giving the peak.
A proton with n equivalent neighbouring protons will appear as a peak split into n+1 sub-peaks.
Standard electrode potentials are measured by submerging the electrode in pure water.
